Let $(V,K)$ be an abstract simplicial complex. Its **geometric realization**
$|K|$ is the set of functions $\alpha:V \to [0,1]$ such that:

1. $\alpha(v)=0$ for all but finitely many $v \in V$;
2. $\sum_{v \in V}\alpha(v)=1$;
3. the support $\operatorname{supp}(\alpha):=\{v \in V:\alpha(v)\neq 0\}$ is a simplex of $K$.

For each simplex $\sigma=\{v_0,\dots,v_n\}$ of $K$, write
$$|\sigma|:=\{\alpha \in |K| : \operatorname{supp}(\alpha)\subseteq \sigma\}.$$
Sending $\alpha$ to the barycentric tuple
$(\alpha(v_0),\dots,\alpha(v_n))$ identifies $|\sigma|$ with the geometric
simplex spanned by the standard basis vectors indexed by $v_0,\dots,v_n$, so
$|\sigma|$ carries its Euclidean simplex topology.

We give $|K|$ the **weak topology** with respect to these simplex inclusions:
a subset $U\subseteq |K|$ is declared open exactly when $U\cap|\sigma|$ is open
in $|\sigma|$ for every simplex $\sigma$ of $K$.

Let $(V,K)$ be an abstract simplicial complex.

A **subcomplex** of $K$ is a subfamily $L \subseteq K$ that is itself closed
under taking subsets.

If $\sigma \in K$, its **closure** is the subcomplex
$$\overline{\sigma}:=\{\tau \in K : \tau \subseteq \sigma\}.$$
More generally, if $A \subseteq K$, its closure is
$$\overline{A}:=\{\tau \in K : \tau \subseteq \sigma \text{ for some } \sigma \in A\}.$$

For a simplex $\sigma \in K$, the **closed star** of $\sigma$ in $K$ is
$$\operatorname{St}_K(\sigma):=\{\tau \in K : \sigma \cup \tau \in K\},$$
and the **open star** is the union, after realization, of the relative
interiors of simplices $\rho\in K$ with $\sigma\subseteq\rho$.

The **link** of $\sigma$ in $K$ is
$$\operatorname{Lk}_K(\sigma):=\{\tau \in K : \tau \cap \sigma=\varnothing \text{ and } \sigma \cup \tau \in K\}.$$

If $K$ is a finite abstract simplicial complex, then its geometric realization
$|K|$ is compact and Hausdorff.

Let $\mathcal F$ be a presheaf on a topological space $X$. We say that
$\mathcal F$ is a **sheaf** if for every open set $U \subseteq X$ and every
open cover $U=\bigcup_{i\in I}U_i$, including the empty cover of
$\varnothing$, the following two conditions hold.

**Locality.** If $s,t\in\mathcal F(U)$ satisfy
$$s|_{U_i}=t|_{U_i}\qquad\text{for all }i\in I,$$
then $s=t$.

**Gluing.** If sections $s_i\in\mathcal F(U_i)$ satisfy
$$s_i|_{U_i\cap U_j}=s_j|_{U_i\cap U_j}\qquad\text{for all }i,j\in I,$$
then there exists $s\in\mathcal F(U)$ such that
$$s|_{U_i}=s_i\qquad\text{for all }i\in I.$$

By locality, such a section $s$ is automatically unique. Thus a sheaf is
exactly a presheaf whose compatible local sections glue uniquely.

Let $X$ be a topological space. A **presheaf of sets on $X$** is a
contravariant functor
$$\mathcal F:\operatorname{Open}(X)\longrightarrow \mathbf{Set}$$
([[def-functor-and-contravariant-functor]],
[[prop-sets-and-functions-form-category-set]]).

Equivalently, a presheaf of sets on $X$ consists of:

- a set $\mathcal F(U)$ for every open set $U \subseteq X$;
- for every inclusion $V \subseteq U$, a restriction map
  $$\rho^U_V:\mathcal F(U)\longrightarrow \mathcal F(V),$$

such that
$$\rho^U_U=\operatorname{id}_{\mathcal F(U)}$$
and, whenever $W \subseteq V \subseteq U$,
$$\rho^U_W=\rho^V_W\circ \rho^U_V.$$

Because the arrows of $\operatorname{Open}(X)$ are the inclusions
$V \to U$ with $V \subseteq U$, contravariance is exactly the rule that sections
over a larger open set restrict to sections over a smaller one.

Let $X$ be a topological space.
Fix a ring $R$ when modules are under discussion.

A **presheaf of groups** on $X$ is a presheaf $\mathcal F$ such that every
$\mathcal F(U)$ is a group and every restriction map
$\rho^U_V:\mathcal F(U)\to\mathcal F(V)$ is a group homomorphism
([[prop-groups-and-homomorphisms-form-category-grp]]).

A **presheaf of rings** on $X$ is defined the same way with rings and ring
homomorphisms ([[prop-rings-and-homomorphisms-form-category-ring]]).

A **presheaf of left $R$-modules** on $X$ is defined the same way with left
$R$-modules and $R$-linear maps
([[prop-modules-and-homomorphisms-form-category-rmod]]).

A **sheaf of groups**, **sheaf of rings**, or **sheaf of left $R$-modules** is
such a presheaf whose underlying set-valued presheaf is a sheaf.

In particular, each sheaf of groups has a distinguished identity section on
every open set; in additive notation this section is written $0$, and all
restrictions preserve the algebraic operations.

Let $(X,\mathcal O_X)$ be a ringed space.

An **$\mathcal O_X$-module** is a sheaf $\mathcal F$ of abelian groups on $X$
such that for every open set $U \subseteq X$ the section group $\mathcal F(U)$
is an $\mathcal O_X(U)$-module, and for every inclusion $V \subseteq U$ the
restriction map
$$
\mathcal F(U)\longrightarrow\mathcal F(V)
$$
is $\mathcal O_X(U)$-linear after restricting scalars along
$\mathcal O_X(U)\to\mathcal O_X(V)$.

A **morphism of $\mathcal O_X$-modules** is a morphism of the underlying sheaves
of abelian groups whose components are $\mathcal O_X(U)$-linear on every open
set $U$.

Let $X$ be a topological space.

1. The category of sheaves of abelian groups on $X$ is an abelian category.
2. If $(X,\mathcal O_X)$ is a ringed space, then the category of
   $\mathcal O_X$-modules is also an abelian category.

Let $\mathcal F$ be a presheaf on a topological space $X$, and let $x\in X$.

The **neighbourhood category of $x$** is the full subcategory
$$\mathcal N_x\subseteq \operatorname{Open}(X)$$
whose objects are the open neighbourhoods of $x$. Its opposite category is
filtered in the sense of
[[def-filtered-category-and-filtered-colimit]]: it is nonempty because $X$
itself is a neighbourhood of $x$, and for neighbourhoods $U,V$ the
intersection $U\cap V$ is again a neighbourhood of $x$ with arrows
$$U\longrightarrow U\cap V,\qquad V\longrightarrow U\cap V$$
in the opposite category.

Because $\mathcal F$ is contravariant, its restriction to the neighbourhood
category determines a covariant diagram on that opposite category. The
**stalk** of $\mathcal F$ at $x$ is the filtered colimit
$$\mathcal F_x:=\varinjlim_{\mathcal N_x^{\operatorname{op}}}\mathcal F(U).$$

Concretely, $\mathcal F_x$ may be described as equivalence classes of pairs
$(U,s)$ with $U$ an open neighbourhood of $x$ and
$s\in\mathcal F(U)$, where $(U,s)\sim(V,t)$ when $s$ and $t$ agree on some
smaller open neighbourhood of $x$. The next lemma verifies that this is an
equivalence relation.

Let
$$
\cdots\longrightarrow \mathcal F_{i-1}\xrightarrow{d_{i-1}}\mathcal F_i\xrightarrow{d_i}\mathcal F_{i+1}\longrightarrow\cdots
$$
be a sequence of sheaves of abelian groups on a topological space $X$. Then the
sequence is exact if and only if, for every point $x\in X$, the stalk sequence
$$
\cdots\longrightarrow (\mathcal F_{i-1})_x\xrightarrow{(d_{i-1})_x}(\mathcal F_i)_x\xrightarrow{(d_i)_x}(\mathcal F_{i+1})_x\longrightarrow\cdots
$$
is exact.

Let $\varphi:\mathcal F\to\mathcal G$ be a morphism of sheaves of sets on a
topological space $X$. Then $\varphi$ is an isomorphism if and only if, for
every $x\in X$, the induced map on stalks
$$\varphi_x:\mathcal F_x\longrightarrow\mathcal G_x$$
is a bijection.

Let $f:X\to Y$ be a continuous map, and let $\mathcal G$ be a presheaf on $Y$.
The **inverse-image presheaf**
$$
f_{\mathrm p}\mathcal G
$$
on $X$ is defined by
$$
(f_{\mathrm p}\mathcal G)(U):=\varinjlim_{f(U)\subseteq V}\mathcal G(V),
$$
where $V$ runs over the open neighbourhoods of $f(U)$ in $Y$, ordered by
reverse inclusion. If $U' \subseteq U$, then every neighbourhood of $f(U)$ is a
neighbourhood of $f(U')$, so there is a natural restriction map
$(f_{\mathrm p}\mathcal G)(U)\to(f_{\mathrm p}\mathcal G)(U')$.

The **inverse image sheaf** of a sheaf $\mathcal G$ on $Y$ is the sheafification
of this presheaf:
$$
f^{-1}\mathcal G:=a(f_{\mathrm p}\mathcal G).
$$

When $U$ is open in $X$ and $V$ is an open set of $Y$ with $f(U)\subseteq V$,
there is a canonical map
$$
\mathcal G(V)\longrightarrow(f_{\mathrm p}\mathcal G)(U)
$$
into the colimit class represented by $V$.

Let $f:X\to Y$ be a continuous map, let $\mathcal G$ be a sheaf on $Y$, and let
$\mathcal F$ be a sheaf on $X$. Then there is a natural bijection
$$\operatorname{Hom}_X(f^{-1}\mathcal G,\mathcal F) \cong \operatorname{Hom}_Y(\mathcal G,f_*\mathcal F).$$

Let $f:X\to Y$ be a continuous map, let $\mathcal G$ be a sheaf on $Y$, and let
$x\in X$. Then there is a canonical isomorphism
$$
(f^{-1}\mathcal G)_x\cong \mathcal G_{f(x)}.
$$

Let $f:X\to Y$ be a continuous map, and let $\mathcal F$ be a presheaf on $X$.
The **direct image presheaf**
$$f_*\mathcal F$$
on $Y$ is defined on an open set $V \subseteq Y$ by
$$
(f_*\mathcal F)(V):=\mathcal F(f^{-1}(V)).
$$
If $V' \subseteq V$, the restriction map
$$
(f_*\mathcal F)(V)\longrightarrow(f_*\mathcal F)(V')
$$
is the restriction map of $\mathcal F$ for the inclusion
$f^{-1}(V') \subseteq f^{-1}(V)$.

Thus direct image is just precomposition of the presheaf with the inverse-image
map on open sets.

Let $f:X\to Y$ be a continuous map.

1. If $\mathcal F$ is a sheaf on $X$, then $f_*\mathcal F$ is a sheaf on $Y$.
2. If $\mathcal F$ is a sheaf of groups, rings, or modules on $X$, then
   $f_*\mathcal F$ is a sheaf of the same kind on $Y$.

Let $j:U\hookrightarrow X$ be the inclusion of an open subspace, and let
$\mathcal F$ be a sheaf on $X$. The **restriction of $\mathcal F$ to $U$** is
the inverse image sheaf
$$
\mathcal F|_U:=j^{-1}\mathcal F.
$$

For an open set $W \subseteq U$, one may identify $(\mathcal F|_U)(W)$ with
$\mathcal F(W)$: because $U$ is open in $X$, the set $W$ is also open in $X$,
and in the neighbourhood-colimit defining $j^{-1}\mathcal F$ the open set $W$
itself is a neighbourhood of $j(W)=W$.

Let $j:U\hookrightarrow X$ be the inclusion of an open subspace, and let
$\mathcal F$ be a sheaf of abelian groups on $U$.

For an open set $V \subseteq X$, define
$$(j_!\mathcal F)(V) := \left\{ s\in \mathcal F(V\cap U): \operatorname{Supp}(s)\text{ is closed in }V \right\}.$$
Equivalently, $s$ lies in $(j_!\mathcal F)(V)$ exactly when for every
$x\in V\setminus U$ there exists an open neighbourhood $W_x \subseteq V$ with
$$
s|_{W_x\cap U}=0.
$$

Restriction maps are inherited from $\mathcal F$, so $j_!\mathcal F$ is a
subsheaf of $j_*\mathcal F$. When $V \subseteq U$, the support condition is
vacuous and
$$
(j_!\mathcal F)(V)=\mathcal F(V).
$$

This is the **extension by zero** of $\mathcal F$ along $j$. It is distinct in
general from the ordinary direct image $j_*\mathcal F$.

Let $j:U\hookrightarrow X$ be the inclusion of an open subspace.

1. For every sheaf of abelian groups $\mathcal F$ on $U$ and every sheaf of
   abelian groups $\mathcal G$ on $X$, there is a natural bijection
   $$\operatorname{Hom}_X(j_!\mathcal F,\mathcal G) \cong \operatorname{Hom}_U(\mathcal F,j^{-1}\mathcal G).$$
2. The functor $j_!$ is exact on sheaves of abelian groups.

Let $S$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]), let $k$ be a field
and let $\mathcal F$ be a sheaf of $k$-vector spaces on $S$
([[def-sheaf-on-topological-space]],
[[def-presheaf-of-groups-rings-modules]]). Then $\mathcal F$ is **locally
constant of finite rank** if every point $x\in S$ has an open neighbourhood
$U\subseteq S$ for which there are an integer $n\ge0$ and an isomorphism of
sheaves on $U$
$$\mathcal F|_U\;\cong\;k_U^{\,n},$$
where $k_U$ is the constant sheaf on $U$ with value $k$ and $\mathcal F|_U$ is
the restriction of $\mathcal F$ to the open subspace $U$
([[def-restriction-sheaf-open-subspace]], [[def-morphism-of-presheaves]],
[[lem-constant-sheaf-is-the-sheaf-of-locally-constant-functions]]). A sheaf with
this property is also called a **finite-rank local system of $k$-vector spaces**
on $S$. This is a property of the sheaf on the space; no identification of such
sheaves with functors on the fundamental groupoid is part of the definition.

The sheaf $k_U^{\,n}$ is the $n$-fold direct sum of $k_U$ in the category of
sheaves of $k$-vector spaces, with $k_U^{\,0}$ the zero sheaf; its sections over
an open $W\subseteq U$ are the locally constant functions $W\to k^n$. The
integer $n$ is quantified locally, so no global rank is asserted and the rank
may differ from point to point; the definition asserts no existence of a global
trivialization. The final sentence records only that a functorial groupoid
presentation of local systems is a different, uncompared object here.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $X$ be a metric space
([[def-metric-space]]) having a neighbourhood basis of contractible open sets at
every point, and let $k$ be a field. Write $k_X$ for its constant sheaf. There
are natural isomorphisms
$$H^q(X,k_X)\cong H^q_{\operatorname{sing}}(X;k)$$
in every degree, where the left side is derived cohomology in the category of
sheaves of $k$-vector spaces (computed with the functorial $k$-linear injective
resolutions supplied by
[[lem-ringed-space-module-sheaves-enough-injectives]]; compare
[[def-sheaf-cohomology-derived-global-sections]]). The same assertion holds on
every open subset of $X$. In particular a nonempty contractible space with this
local property has constant-sheaf cohomology $k$ in degree zero and zero
otherwise. This applies to every finite-polyhedral open star and to its
nonempty intersection with a closed simplex.

Let $i:Z\hookrightarrow X$ be the inclusion of a closed subset
$Z\subseteq X$ carrying the subspace topology ([[def-subspace-topology-top]]), and
let $\mathcal G$ be a sheaf of abelian groups on $X$
([[def-sheaf-on-topological-space]], [[thm-abelian-sheaves-form-abelian-category]])
whose stalks vanish off $Z$, that is $\mathcal G_x=0$ for every $x\in X\setminus Z$
([[def-stalk-of-presheaf]]). Then the unit
$$\eta:\mathcal G\longrightarrow i_*i^{-1}\mathcal G$$
of the adjunction ([[thm-inverse-direct-image-adjunction]]) between inverse image
and direct image ([[def-direct-image-sheaf]], [[lem-direct-image-is-sheaf]]) is an
isomorphism of sheaves of abelian groups; equivalently
$\mathcal G\cong i_*(\mathcal G|_Z)$ under the identification
$\mathcal G|_Z=i^{-1}\mathcal G$ ([[def-restriction-sheaf-open-subspace]]).

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $Z\subseteq X$
be a closed subset of a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]), equipped
with the subspace topology ([[def-subspace-topology-top]]), let
$i:Z\hookrightarrow X$ be the inclusion, and let $\mathcal F$ be a sheaf of
abelian groups on $Z$ ([[def-sheaf-on-topological-space]]). Then for every
$q\ge0$ there is an isomorphism
$$H^q(Z,\mathcal F)\cong H^q(X,i_*\mathcal F),$$
where $i_*\mathcal F$ is the direct image sheaf
([[def-direct-image-sheaf]], [[lem-direct-image-is-sheaf]]) and cohomology is
that of [[def-sheaf-cohomology-derived-global-sections]].

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Fix a topological space $X$, let
$$\Gamma(X,-):\mathrm{Ab}(X)\to\mathbf{Ab}$$
be the additive left exact global-sections functor
([[def-global-sections-functor-sheaves]]), and let $I$ be the supplied
functorial injective resolution datum on $\mathrm{Ab}(X)$ of
[[thm-abelian-sheaves-have-enough-injectives]]: it assigns to every abelian
sheaf $\mathcal F$ one specific injective resolution
$0\to\mathcal F\to I^\bullet(\mathcal F)$
([[def-right-derived-object-relative-to-injective-resolution-data]]).

For every $q\ge0$ and every abelian sheaf $\mathcal F$ on $X$ define the
**$q$-th sheaf cohomology group of $\mathcal F$** to be the right derived
object of $\Gamma(X,-)$ relative to $I$:
$$H^q(X,\mathcal F):=R_I^q\Gamma(X,\mathcal F)=H^q\bigl(\Gamma(X,I^\bullet(\mathcal F)_{\mathrm{del}})\bigr),$$
the cohomology object of the complex
$\Gamma(X,I^0(\mathcal F))\to\Gamma(X,I^1(\mathcal F))\to\cdots$ of abelian
groups obtained from the deleted resolution
([[def-deleted-resolution]], [[def-cohomology-object-of-a-cochain-complex]]).
We also set $H^q(X,\mathcal F):=0$ for $q<0$.

Because $I$ is a fixed supplied datum, the group $H^q(X,\mathcal F)$ is a
specific group for each pair $(X,\mathcal F)$, and for a morphism
$\varphi:\mathcal F\to\mathcal G$ of abelian sheaves we write
$H^q(X,\varphi):=R_I^q\Gamma(X,\varphi)$ for the induced map; it is the map on
cohomology induced by $\Gamma(X,-)$ applied to the cochain maps supplied with
the datum, and it is additive in $\varphi$.

If $J$ is another supplied injective resolution datum on $\mathrm{Ab}(X)$ then
$R_I^q\Gamma(X,-)$ and $R_J^q\Gamma(X,-)$ are naturally isomorphic, so the
$H^q(X,\mathcal F)$ computed from $J$ agree with the ones above up to a
canonical natural isomorphism; the Axiom of Dependent Choice needed for that
comparison follows from AC
([[thm-right-derived-functors-from-two-supplied-injective-resolution-data-are-naturally-isomorphic]],
[[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]]). The notation
$H^q(X,\mathcal F)$ therefore does not depend on the datum used, up to this
canonical isomorphism, and we call $q$ the **cohomological degree**.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $X$ be a
topological space, let $H^q(X,-)$ be sheaf cohomology computed from the supplied
functorial injective resolution datum $I$ of
[[thm-abelian-sheaves-have-enough-injectives]]
([[def-sheaf-cohomology-derived-global-sections]]), and let
$\mathbb Z_X$ be the constant sheaf with value $\mathbb Z$
([[lem-constant-sheaf-is-the-sheaf-of-locally-constant-functions]]). Under the
standing smallness or supplied cofinal-denominator hypothesis of
[[def-derived-category-of-an-abelian-category]], for every abelian sheaf
$\mathcal F$ on $X$ and every $p\ge0$ there is a canonical isomorphism
$$\operatorname{Hom}_{D(\mathrm{Ab}(X))}(\mathbb Z_X[-p],\mathcal F)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }H^p(X,\mathcal F),$$
exhibited by the chain
$$\operatorname{Hom}_D(\mathbb Z_X[-p],\mathcal F) \longrightarrow\operatorname{Hom}_D(\mathbb Z_X[-p],I^\bullet(\mathcal F)) \xleftarrow{\ Q\ }\operatorname{Hom}_K(\mathbb Z_X[-p],I^\bullet(\mathcal F)) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }H^0\bigl(\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}^\bullet(\mathbb Z_X[-p],I^\bullet(\mathcal F))\bigr) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }H^p(X,\mathcal F),$$
where the first arrow is composition with $Q(\eta_{\mathcal F})$ for the
coaugmentation $\eta_{\mathcal F}:\mathcal F\to I^\bullet(\mathcal F)$ of the
datum, the second is the localization map $Q$ of
[[def-derived-category-of-an-abelian-category]], and the last two identify the
full Hom complex with the shift $\Gamma(X,I^\bullet(\mathcal F))[p]$, including the negative degrees that supply boundaries in degree zero. Moreover:

1. **(Naturality and additivity.)** The isomorphism is additive and natural in
   $\mathcal F$: for every morphism $\psi:\mathcal F\to\mathcal G$ of abelian
   sheaves the square
   $$\begin{matrix} \operatorname{Hom}_D(\mathbb Z_X[-p],\mathcal F)&\longrightarrow&H^p(X,\mathcal F)\\ \downarrow\scriptstyle{\circ Q(\psi)}&&\downarrow\scriptstyle{H^p(X,\psi)}\\ \operatorname{Hom}_D(\mathbb Z_X[-p],\mathcal G)&\longrightarrow&H^p(X,\mathcal G) \end{matrix}$$
   commutes, $H^p(X,\psi)$ being the map induced by $\Gamma(X,\psi)$ on the
   cochain maps supplied with the datum
   ([[def-sheaf-cohomology-derived-global-sections]]).

2. **(Degree zero.)** For $p=0$ the composite of the isomorphism with the
   canonical isomorphism $H^0(X,\mathcal F)\xrightarrow{\sim}\Gamma(X,\mathcal F)$
   of [[thm-zero-sheaf-cohomology-global-sections]] is the bijection
   $\varphi\mapsto\varphi_X(1_X)$ of
   [[lem-morphisms-from-the-constant-sheaf-are-global-sections]]; in particular
   the identity of $\mathbb Z_X$ corresponds to $1_X\in\Gamma(X,\mathbb Z_X)$.

Let $P$ be a finite nonempty poset, regarded as a category with one arrow $p\to q$ exactly when $p\le q$, and let $h$ be the largest number of strict inequalities in a chain of $P$. Let $\operatorname{Diag}_k(P)$ be the abelian category of covariant diagrams of $k$-vector spaces on $P$, i.e. the functor category of $k$-vector spaces indexed by $P$, with its cochain complexes as in [[def-cochain-complex-in-an-abelian-category]]. If $M$ is a bounded complex of diagrams in $\operatorname{Diag}_k(P)$ whose vector spaces are finite-dimensional and vanish outside internal degrees $[a,b]$, then the derived inverse limit $\mathbf R\lim M:=\mathbf R\operatorname{Hom}(\underline k,M)$ ([[def-derived-hom-in-the-bounded-setting]]) has a finite-dimensional cochain model concentrated in $[a,b+h]$. If $A,B$ are such complexes, concentrated in $[a,b]$ and $[c,d]$ respectively, then their derived Hom has a finite-dimensional cochain model concentrated in $[c-b,d-a+h]$. These models commute with every field extension. For the empty poset, the diagram sections and the derived Hom model are zero by convention.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $X$ be a topological
space and let $k$ be a field. The category $\operatorname{Sh}_k(X)$ of sheaves
of $k$-vector spaces is the category of modules over the ringed space
$(X,k_X)$ with constant structure sheaf $k_X$
([[def-locally-ringed-space]], [[def-module-on-ringed-space]]); it is a locally
small Grothendieck category and carries a functorial injective embedding, and
iterating that embedding on cokernels yields for every $k$-sheaf one specific
injective resolution
([[lem-ringed-space-module-sheaves-enough-injectives]]). Every bounded-below
complex also has a bounded-below termwise injective replacement
([[lem-bounded-below-complexes-admit-injective-replacements]]). With the dependent choice supplied by
AC ([[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]]) the bounded-below
injective complexes model the bounded-below derived category:
$K^+(\operatorname{Inj}\operatorname{Sh}_k(X))\to
D^+(\operatorname{Sh}_k(X))$ is an equivalence
([[thm-injective-complexes-model-the-bounded-below-derived-category]]).
Its full subcategory of bounded-below injective complexes with bounded
cohomology models $D^b(\operatorname{Sh}_k(X))$, and morphisms of the bounded
derived category are computed by these replacements; the replacements need
not have bounded terms.

Now let $X$ be a separated finite-type complex algebraic variety and let
$\mathfrak S$ be a finite smooth algebraic stratification with the frontier
condition of $X$
([[def-analytic-topology-and-finite-smooth-algebraic-stratifications]]). Let
$D^b_{\mathfrak S}(X;k)$ be the full subcategory of
$D^b(\operatorname{Sh}_k(X))$ of complexes whose cohomology sheaves are bounded
and constructible with respect to $\mathfrak S$
([[def-algebraically-constructible-complex-of-analytic-field-sheaves]]). Then
$D^b_{\mathfrak S}(X;k)$ is a triangulated subcategory: it is closed under
shifts, isomorphisms and mapping cones. More generally, if two bounded
algebraically constructible complexes are constructible with respect to one
common finite smooth algebraic frontier stratification, then their cone is
bounded and constructible with respect to that stratification.

With supplied bounded-below injective replacements $j_X:X\to I_X$ (and DC or supplied homotopy extensions), $K^+(\operatorname{Inj}\mathcal A)\to D^+(\mathcal A)$ is an equivalence of triangulated categories. For a bounded-below complex $I$, K-injectivity can be tested using only bounded-below acyclic inputs.
A bounded-below cochain complex $I$ of injective objects is K-injective. Assume dependent choice for the countable successive homotopy extensions, or supply those extensions as data.

A cochain complex $I$ is **homotopically injective**, or **K-injective**, if $\operatorname{Hom}_K(A,I[r])=0$ for every acyclic cochain complex $A$ and every integer $r$. Equivalently, $\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}(A,I)$ is acyclic. This uses the Hom complex and shifted Hom identification fixed in [[def-homotopically-projective-bounded-above-complex]]. A **bounded-below K-injective complex** additionally has $I^n=0$ for all sufficiently negative $n$. The K-injective property itself neither assumes boundedness nor means termwise injectivity.

For a K-injective complex $I$ and any complex $X$, $Q:\operatorname{Hom}_K(X,I)\to\operatorname{Hom}_D(X,I)$ is bijective. Moreover, if $s:I\to J$ is a quasi-isomorphism, its cone triangle is split in $K$: $J\cong I\oplus\operatorname{Cone}(s)$ with $s$ corresponding to the inclusion.

For cochain complexes put $\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}^r(P,A)=\prod_n\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal A}(P^n,A^{n+r})$, with $(du)^n=d_Au^n-(-1)^ru^{n+1}d_P$. This is the reindexing of [[def-hom-complex-of-chain-complexes]]. A complex $P$ is **homotopically projective**, or **K-projective**, if $\operatorname{Hom}_K(P,A[r])=0$ for every acyclic complex $A$ and every integer $r$. Equivalently $\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}(P,A)$ is acyclic: the degree-zero Hom/homotopy identification of [[thm-hom-in-the-homotopy-category-is-zero-degree-homology-of-the-hom-complex]], applied after shifting $A$, identifies these groups with its cohomology (a boundary differs only by the invertible sign $(-1)^r$).

The bounded-above case additionally requires $P^n=0$ for all sufficiently large $n$, as in [[def-bounded-bounded-below-and-bounded-above-complex]]. Boundedness is not part of the general K-projective predicate. Nor is termwise projectivity: a contractible complex has zero Hom from it in $K$ and is K-projective irrespective of its terms.
A bounded-above cochain complex $P$ of projective objects is K-projective. Assume dependent choice for the countable successive homotopy choices, or supply those lifts as data.
For a K-projective complex $P$ and any complex $X$, $Q:\operatorname{Hom}_K(P,X)\to\operatorname{Hom}_D(P,X)$ is bijective, under the standing localization size convention.

Assume the Axiom of Dependent Choice.

Let $I$ be a supplied injective resolution datum on a class $\mathcal D$, let
$F:\mathcal A\to\mathcal B$ be an additive left exact functor, and let
$$0\to A\to J^0\to J^1\to J^2\to\cdots$$
be an $F$-acyclic resolution of $A$ relative to $I$. Assume moreover that
$A\in\mathcal D$ and that, for $Z^0:=A$ and
$$0\to Z^q\to J^q\to Z^{q+1}\to0\qquad(q\ge0),$$
each $Z^q$ lies in $\mathcal D$. Then for every $n\ge 0$ there is a canonical
isomorphism
$$R_I^nF(A)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }H^n(F(J^\bullet_{\mathrm{del}})).$$

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

For a cochain complex $X$, define the **canonical truncations** by

$$ (\tau^{\leq n}X)^i=\begin{cases}X^i&i<n,\\\ker d_X^n&i=n,\\0&i>n,\end{cases}\qquad (\tau^{\geq n}X)^i=\begin{cases}0&i<n,\\\operatorname{coker}d_X^{n-1}&i=n,\\X^i&i>n.\end{cases} $$

The differential into $\ker d_X^n$ is the factorization of $d_X^{n-1}$; the differential out of $\operatorname{coker}d_X^{n-1}$ is induced by $d_X^n$. All other retained differentials are those of $X$. There are natural maps $\tau^{\leq n}X\to X\to\tau^{\geq n}X$. Unlike [[def-brutal-truncation-of-a-complex]], these constructions correct the boundary using the cycle and boundary objects of [[def-cohomology-object-of-a-cochain-complex]].

Every short exact sequence $0\to A\xrightarrow iB\xrightarrow qC\to0$ of cochain complexes gives a natural distinguished triangle $A\to B\to C\to A[1]$ in $D(\mathcal A)$. In particular, for every integer $n$ there are canonical distinguished triangles

$$\tau^{\leq n}X\to X\to\tau^{\geq n+1}X\to(\tau^{\leq n}X)[1],$$

$$\tau^{\leq n}X\to\tau^{\leq n+1}X\to H^{n+1}(X)[-n-1]\to(\tau^{\leq n}X)[1],$$

$$H^n(X)[-n]\to\tau^{\geq n}X\to\tau^{\geq n+1}X\to H^n(X)[-n+1].$$

The derived category, with shift $[1]$ and distinguished triangles the isomorphic images of cone triangles, is triangulated. The localization functor $Q$ is exact. Every such triangle gives a long exact cohomology sequence $\cdots\to H^n(X)\to H^n(Y)\to H^n(Z)\to H^{n+1}(X)\to\cdots$.

The canonical functors $D^-(\mathcal A),D^+(\mathcal A),D^b(\mathcal A)\to D(\mathcal A)$ are fully faithful and exact. Their essential images consist exactly of complexes with cohomology respectively bounded above, bounded below, or bounded on both sides.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $X$ be a locally
compact Hausdorff space, let $\mathrm{Ab}(X)$ be the category of sheaves of
abelian groups on $X$ ([[def-sheaf-on-topological-space]]) and let
$$\Gamma(X,-):\mathrm{Ab}(X)\longrightarrow\mathbf{Ab}$$
be the additive left exact global-sections functor
([[def-global-sections-functor-sheaves]],
[[def-section-restriction-and-global-section]]). For a sheaf $\mathcal F$ on
$X$ define the **compactly supported global sections** of $\mathcal F$ to be the
subgroup
$$\Gamma_c(X,\mathcal F):=\{\,s\in\Gamma(X,\mathcal F):\operatorname{Supp}(s)\ \text{is a compact subset of }X\,\}\subseteq\Gamma(X,\mathcal F),$$
where the support of a section is the set of points at which its germ is
nonzero ([[def-support-of-a-sheaf-section]], [[def-germ-of-section]],
[[def-compact-space]]). This is a subgroup: the zero section has empty support, negation preserves
support, and the support of a sum is closed in $X$ and contained in the finite
union of the two compact supports, hence compact
([[def-support-of-a-sheaf-section]],
[[thm-closed-subspace-of-a-compact-space-is-compact]]).
A morphism $\varphi:\mathcal F\to\mathcal G$ of abelian
sheaves induces a map $\Gamma_c(X,\varphi)$ by restriction of
$\Gamma(X,\varphi)$, and this makes $\Gamma_c(X,-)$ an additive functor
$\mathrm{Ab}(X)\to\mathbf{Ab}$ ([[def-additive-functor]],
[[def-morphism-of-presheaves]]). Six consistency facts hold; all are immediate
from the definitions, and they record the interface used by the compact-support
calculus.

1. **Well-definedness of $\Gamma_c(X,\varphi)$.** If $x\notin
   \operatorname{Supp}(s)$ then $s_x=0$ in the stalk $\mathcal F_x$
   ([[def-stalk-of-presheaf]]), and since the stalk maps of a morphism commute
   with the germ maps, $\varphi(s)_x=\varphi_x(s_x)=0$, so
   $\operatorname{Supp}(\varphi(s))\subseteq\operatorname{Supp}(s)$. A support
   $\operatorname{Supp}(t)$ is closed in $X$: if $x\notin
   \operatorname{Supp}(t)$ then $t$ agrees with the zero section on some open
   neighbourhood of $x$, by the description of equality of germs
   ([[def-support-of-a-sheaf-section]]). Hence
   $\operatorname{Supp}(\varphi(s))$ is a closed subset of $X$ contained in the
   compact set $\operatorname{Supp}(s)$; being closed in $X$ it is closed in the
   subspace $\operatorname{Supp}(s)$, so it is a compact subset of that compact
   space ([[thm-closed-subspace-of-a-compact-space-is-compact]]) and therefore
   a compact subset of $X$ ([[lem-compactness-of-a-subspace-is-ambient]]), and
   $\Gamma_c(X,\varphi)$ maps $\Gamma_c(X,\mathcal F)$ into
   $\Gamma_c(X,\mathcal G)$. Composites and identities are computed
   componentwise, so $\Gamma_c(X,-)$ is a functor; it is additive because
   $\Gamma(X,-)$ is.
2. **Sheaves of $k$-vector spaces.** If $\mathcal F$ is a sheaf of
   $k$-vector spaces, then $\Gamma_c(X,\mathcal F)$ is a $k$-vector subspace of
   $\Gamma(X,\mathcal F)$: the support of $c\cdot s$ is
   $\operatorname{Supp}(s)$ for $c\ne0$ and $\varnothing$ for $c=0$, and the
   zero section has empty support. For a morphism $\varphi$ of sheaves of
   $k$-vector spaces the map $\Gamma_c(X,\varphi)$ is $k$-linear, since
   $\Gamma(X,\varphi)$ is. The higher derived functors below are computed from
   an injective resolution datum on abelian sheaves, so they are abelian
   groups; the degree-zero part is the $k$-vector space
   $\Gamma_c(X,\mathcal F)$.
3. **Left exactness.** For every short exact sequence
   $0\to\mathcal F'\xrightarrow{\varphi'}\mathcal F\xrightarrow{\varphi}\mathcal F''\to0$
   of abelian sheaves the sequence
   $$0\to\Gamma_c(X,\mathcal F')\xrightarrow{\Gamma_c(\varphi')}\Gamma_c(X,\mathcal F)\xrightarrow{\Gamma_c(\varphi)}\Gamma_c(X,\mathcal F'')$$
   is exact. Injectivity: a monomorphism of sheaves has injective stalk maps
   ([[thm-exactness-of-sheaves-stalkwise]]), so
   $\operatorname{Supp}(\varphi'(s'))=\operatorname{Supp}(s')$ and a section
   killed by $\varphi'$ has all germs zero, hence is zero. Exactness at the
   middle: the kernel of $\Gamma(X,\varphi)$ is the image of
   $\Gamma(X,\varphi')$ by left exactness of global sections
   ([[lem-global-sections-left-exact]]); if $s=\varphi'(s')$ has compact
   support, then $s'$ has the same support,
   $\operatorname{Supp}(s')=\operatorname{Supp}(\varphi'(s'))=
   \operatorname{Supp}(s)$, because $\varphi'$ is stalk-injective, so $s'$ lies
   in $\Gamma_c(X,\mathcal F')$, and the reverse inclusion is immediate from
   $\varphi\circ\varphi'=0$. Thus $\Gamma_c(X,-)$ is an additive left exact
   functor on $\mathrm{Ab}(X)$ ([[def-left-exact-and-right-exact-functor]]).
4. **The derived functors.** Abelian sheaves on $X$ have enough injectives, and
   the embeddings of [[thm-abelian-sheaves-have-enough-injectives]] supply one
   functorial injective resolution datum $\mathcal F\mapsto I^\bullet(\mathcal F)$
   on the whole category $\mathrm{Ab}(X)$, under the Axiom of Choice
   ([[def-right-derived-object-relative-to-injective-resolution-data]]). The
   **compactly supported cohomology** of $\mathcal F$ is
   $$H^q_c(X,\mathcal F):=R^q\Gamma_c(X,\mathcal F):=H^q\bigl(\Gamma_c(X,I^\bullet(\mathcal F)_{\mathrm{del}})\bigr)\qquad(q\ge0),\qquad H^q_c(X,\mathcal F):=0\quad(q<0),$$
   the cohomology of the deleted resolution, as in the pattern of
   [[def-sheaf-cohomology-derived-global-sections]]; for a morphism $\varphi$ we
   write $H^q_c(X,\varphi):=R^q\Gamma_c(X,\varphi)$ for the induced map.
5. **Independence of the datum.** If $J$ is another supplied injective
   resolution datum on $\mathrm{Ab}(X)$, then $R^q\Gamma_c(X,-)$ computed from
   $J$ is naturally isomorphic to $R^q\Gamma_c(X,-)$ computed from $I$
   ([[thm-right-derived-functors-from-two-supplied-injective-resolution-data-are-naturally-isomorphic]]);
   the Axiom of Dependent Choice needed for that comparison follows from AC
   ([[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]]). The notation
   $H^q_c(X,\mathcal F)$ therefore does not depend on the datum up to this
   canonical natural isomorphism.
6. **Delta functor and the compact case.** Since $\Gamma_c(X,-)$ is additive
   and left exact and the datum is defined on all of $\mathrm{Ab}(X)$, the
   functors $R^q\Gamma_c(X,-)$, $q\ge0$, carry connecting maps that make them a
   cohomological delta functor with $R^0\Gamma_c(X,-)\cong\Gamma_c(X,-)$, and
   every short exact sequence of abelian sheaves has a long exact
   compact-support cohomology sequence, natural in the sequence
   ([[thm-right-derived-functors-form-a-cohomological-delta-functor]]). If $X$
   is compact, then for every global section $s$ its support is closed in $X$ by
   fact 1, hence a closed subset of the compact space $X$ and therefore
   compact, so every global section is compactly supported; hence
   $\Gamma_c(X,-)=\Gamma(X,-)$ and
   $H^q_c(X,\mathcal F)=H^q(X,\mathcal F)$ for every $q$, where $H^q(X,-)$ is
   the sheaf cohomology of [[def-sheaf-cohomology-derived-global-sections]]
   computed from the same datum.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $X$ be a locally compact Hausdorff space and
let $\mathcal F$ be a sheaf of abelian groups on $X$
([[def-sheaf-on-topological-space]]); every clause applies in particular to
sheaves of $k$-vector spaces, and the tensor clause of (4) is stated only
there. Then:

1. if $\mathcal F$ is c-soft ([[def-c-soft-sheaf]]), every section of
   $\mathcal F$ over a compact subset $K\subseteq X$ extends to a compactly
   supported global section whose support is contained in any prescribed open
   neighbourhood of $K$;
2. every injective abelian sheaf on $X$ is c-soft;
3. if $\mathcal F$ is c-soft, then $H^q_c(X,\mathcal F)=0$ for every $q>0$
   ([[def-compactly-supported-global-sections]]); when $X$ is compact this is
   the vanishing of the sheaf cohomology $H^q(X,\mathcal F)$
   ([[def-sheaf-cohomology-derived-global-sections]]);
4. c-softness is preserved by restriction to open subsets, by restriction to
   closed subsets, by extension by zero along an open inclusion, and by finite
   direct sums of sheaves of abelian groups; for sheaves of $k$-vector spaces
   it is also preserved by tensor product with a constant $k$-vector space;
5. if $0\to\mathcal F'\xrightarrow{\alpha}\mathcal F\xrightarrow{\beta}\mathcal F''\to0$
   is a short exact sequence of sheaves of abelian groups and $\mathcal F'$ is
   c-soft, then every section of $\mathcal F''$ over a compact subset lifts to
   a section of $\mathcal F$ over an open neighbourhood of it, and the induced
   sequence
   $0\to\Gamma_c(X,\mathcal F')\to\Gamma_c(X,\mathcal F)\to\Gamma_c(X,\mathcal F'')\to0$
   is exact; if $\mathcal F'$ and $\mathcal F$ are c-soft then
   $\mathcal F''$ is c-soft.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $X$ be a locally compact Hausdorff space, let
$j:U\hookrightarrow X$ be the inclusion of an open subspace with closed
complement $Z=X\setminus U$
([[def-subspace-topology-top]], [[def-locally-compact-space]],
[[def-hausdorff-space]]), and let $i:Z\hookrightarrow X$ be the inclusion of
$Z$. All sheaves below are sheaves of abelian groups
([[def-sheaf-on-topological-space]]); every clause applies in particular to
sheaves of $k$-vector spaces.

1. For every sheaf $\mathcal A$ on $U$ the canonical map
   $\Gamma_c(X,j_!\mathcal A)\to\Gamma_c(U,\mathcal A)$ --- the restriction of
   the identification of $(j_!\mathcal A)(X)$ with a subgroup of
   $\mathcal A(U)$ ([[def-extension-by-zero-abelian-sheaf]],
   [[def-compactly-supported-global-sections]]) --- is an isomorphism, natural
   in $\mathcal A$; the functor $j_!$ carries c-soft sheaves on $U$ to c-soft
   sheaves on $X$ ([[def-c-soft-sheaf]]); and the induced canonical
   isomorphisms $R^q\Gamma_c(X,j_!\mathcal A)\cong R^q\Gamma_c(U,\mathcal A)$
   hold for all $q\ge0$ and are natural in $\mathcal A$.
2. For every sheaf $\mathcal B$ on $Z$ the canonical map
   $\Gamma_c(X,i_*\mathcal B)\to\Gamma_c(Z,\mathcal B)$ --- the restriction of
   the identification of $(i_*\mathcal B)(X)$ with $\mathcal B(Z)$
   ([[def-direct-image-sheaf]], [[lem-direct-image-is-sheaf]]) --- is an
   isomorphism, natural in $\mathcal B$; the functor $i_*$ carries c-soft
   sheaves on $Z$ to c-soft sheaves on $X$; and the induced canonical
   isomorphisms $R^q\Gamma_c(X,i_*\mathcal B)\cong R^q\Gamma_c(Z,\mathcal B)$
   hold for all $q\ge0$ and are natural in $\mathcal B$.
3. If $Z$ is compact ([[def-compact-space]]), then
   $\Gamma_c(X,i_*\mathcal B)\cong\Gamma(Z,\mathcal B)$ and
   $R^q\Gamma_c(X,i_*\mathcal B)\cong H^q(Z,\mathcal B)$ for all $q\ge0$
   ([[def-sheaf-cohomology-derived-global-sections]]).

All isomorphisms are the canonical ones induced by the extension-by-zero
adjunction [[thm-extension-by-zero-adjunction-exactness]] and by the
acyclic-resolution comparison
[[thm-acyclic-resolution-theorem-for-right-derived-functors]]; no choice is
used beyond the injective resolution data and their comparison theorems.

Let $(X,\mathcal O_X)$ be a ringed space, and let $\mathcal F,\mathcal G$ be
$\mathcal O_X$-modules. The **internal Hom sheaf**
$$
\mathcal Hom_{\mathcal O_X}(\mathcal F,\mathcal G)
$$
is the sheaf on $X$ defined by
$$U\longmapsto \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal O_X|_U}(\mathcal F|_U,\mathcal G|_U)$$
for each open set $U \subseteq X$.

Restriction to a smaller open set $V \subseteq U$ sends a morphism
$\mathcal F|_U\to\mathcal G|_U$ to its restriction
$\mathcal F|_V\to\mathcal G|_V$. Multiplication by a local section
$a\in \mathcal O_X(U)$ acts on a morphism $\varphi$ by either pre- or
post-composition with multiplication by $a$, giving
$\mathcal Hom_{\mathcal O_X}(\mathcal F,\mathcal G)$ the structure of an
$\mathcal O_X$-module.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $f:X\to Y$ be a continuous map of topological spaces and let $k$ be a field. Inverse image of sheaves of $k$-vector spaces ([[def-sheaf-on-topological-space]], [[def-inverse-image-presheaf-and-sheaf]]) is exact and $f^*\dashv Rf_*$, where $Rf_*$ is computed on bounded-below $k$-linear injective replacements ([[lem-bounded-below-complexes-admit-injective-replacements]], [[thm-injective-complexes-model-the-bounded-below-derived-category]]). For bounded complexes $A,B$ ([[def-bounded-bounded-below-and-bounded-above-complex]]) the derived tensor over $k$ is their signed total tensor ([[def-sheaf-tensor-product]]), and for bounded $A$ and bounded-below $B$ the derived internal Hom $R\mathcal Hom(A,B)$ is computed by $\mathcal Hom^\bullet(A,I_B)$ in a $k$-linear bounded-below injective model $B\to I_B$ ([[def-sheaf-hom]], [[def-derived-hom-in-the-bounded-setting]]). Flasque $k$-sheaves ([[def-flasque-sheaf]]) are acyclic for sections on every open set ([[def-sheaf-cohomology-derived-global-sections]]). The tensor-Hom adjunction and the dg associativity, evaluation and symmetry identities are natural. No bounded-constructibility claim for the internal Hom is made here; that requires the local geometric supplier of the later constructible items.

Let $\mathcal J$ be a small filtered category
([[def-filtered-category-and-filtered-colimit]]). The filtered colimit functor
$$\operatorname*{colim}_{\mathcal J}:\mathbf{Ab}^{\mathcal J}\to\mathbf{Ab}$$
on abelian groups is exact ([[def-exact-functor-between-abelian-categories]]).
Equivalently:

1. for a $\mathcal J$-indexed diagram of short exact sequences
   $0\to A_j\to B_j\to C_j\to 0$ of abelian groups, the colimit sequence
   $$0\to\operatorname*{colim}_jA_j\to\operatorname*{colim}_jB_j\to\operatorname*{colim}_jC_j\to 0$$
   is short exact;
2. for a $\mathcal J$-indexed diagram of cochain complexes of abelian groups
   $K_j^\bullet$, the canonical map
   $\operatorname*{colim}_jH^p(K_j^\bullet)\to H^p(\operatorname*{colim}_jK_j^\bullet)$
   is an isomorphism for every $p\in\mathbb Z$; in particular the colimit of a
   diagram of exact complexes is exact in every degree.
Assume the Axiom of Choice. For complexes of vector spaces over a field $k$ with finite diagonals, cross product is a natural isomorphism $\bigoplus_{p+q=n}H_pC\otimes_kH_qD\cong H_n(C\otimes_kD)$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $(X,d)$ be a compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]],
[[def-metric-space]]) and let $\mathcal{U}$ be an open cover of $X$. Then there
is a real $\delta > 0$, a **Lebesgue number** for $\mathcal{U}$, such that every
nonempty $A \subseteq X$ with $\operatorname{diam}(A) < \delta$
([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]) satisfies $A \subseteq U$ for some
$U \in \mathcal{U}$.

Diameters of nonempty subsets of $X$ are defined because a compact space is
bounded ([[thm-compact-subset-is-closed-and-bounded]]) and a subset of a bounded
set is bounded. No choice principle is used.

derivations.claim: **The carrier map.** The principal upsets $P_{\ge\sigma}=\{\tau\in P:\tau\supseteq\sigma\}$ form a basis of the Alexandrov topology: a subset is open exactly when it is upward closed, and an upward-closed set is the union of the principal upsets of its elements. Since $D$ is a subcomplex, every face of a simplex in $D$ lies in $D$, so contraposition makes the set $P$ of nonempty simplices outside $D$ upward closed under taking cofaces; hence $q^{-1}(P_{\ge\sigma})=\{x\in X:\sigma\subseteq q(x)\}=\operatorname{St}(\sigma)$, because a point of $|K|$ whose carrier contains $\sigma$ cannot lie in $|D|$ and every coface of a simplex of $P$ again lies in $P$. The star $\operatorname{St}(\sigma)=\bigcup_{\tau\supseteq\sigma}\tau^\circ$ is open in $|K|$, since its trace on each closed simplex $|\eta|$ is $\{x\in|\eta|:\sigma\subseteq\operatorname{supp}(x)\}$, which is relatively open when $\sigma\subseteq\eta$ and empty otherwise; being contained in $X$ it is also open in $X$. As the principal upsets form a basis, $q$ is continuous. Each $\sigma^\circ$ is convex in the affine simplex spanned by $\sigma$, hence connected, locally path-connected and simply connected, and each $\operatorname{St}(\sigma)$ is open and nonempty.

**Exact realization.** A diagram $V:P\to k\text{-}\mathbf{Vect}$ defines a sheaf $U\mapsto\lim_{\sigma\in U}V_\sigma$: compatible families glue uniquely componentwise. The least neighbourhood $P_{\ge\sigma}$ has initial object $\sigma$, so its sections and its stalk are $V_\sigma$. Conversely, a sheaf on $P$ has these values on the principal opens; restrictions give the diagram, and the sheaf axiom recovers its sections on every open. Thus sheaves on $P$ and diagrams are equivalent. Define $\widehat V=q^{-1}V$. Its stalk at $x$ is $V_{q(x)}$, so realization is exact. On $\sigma^\circ$, the carrier factors through the point $\sigma$ of $P$; composition of inverse images identifies its restriction with the constant sheaf of value $V_\sigma$. This constructs the constant-sheaf identification, rather than inferring it from an abstract equality of stalk values.

**Triviality and generization.** First, a finite-rank local system on a convex simplex interior is constant. By [F18], subdivide a path into finitely many intervals lying in trivializing opens and compose their stalk identifications. Refining the subdivision does not change the composite. On overlaps, transition matrices are locally constant, so a further subdivision proves independence of the trivializing opens. A homotopy between paths has compact square domain; subdivide that square finely enough that each small square maps into one trivializing open. Transport around each small square is the identity, and cancellation of its shared edges shows that transport along the two boundary paths agrees. Convexity provides such a homotopy between any two paths with fixed endpoints. Transport from a fixed point therefore defines a sheaf map from its constant stalk sheaf to the local system: near each point it is the identification from one trivialization. It is an isomorphism by the stalk criterion. Put $V_\sigma=F_{b_\sigma}$. For $\sigma\le\tau$, represent a germ at $b_\sigma$ on a sufficiently small ambient Euclidean ball; its intersection with $\tau^\circ$ is nonempty and convex. Extend its restriction uniquely along the constant sheaf on $\tau^\circ$ and evaluate at $b_\tau$. Equal germ representatives agree on a smaller such ball, so this map is well defined and linear. The same construction based at any point of $\sigma^\circ$ is locally constant after the canonical transport identifications: lift finitely many basis germs to ambient sections and shrink so that their values on each of the finitely many cofaces are fixed. Connectedness of $\sigma^\circ$ makes each incidence matrix constant throughout it. For $\sigma\le\eta\le\tau$, choose a point of $\eta^\circ$ in the ball representing the original germ and restrict the same section near that point into $\tau^\circ$; uniqueness of extension and the just-proved independence of the point on $\eta^\circ$ give the transitivity equation. Identities are immediate. This reconstructs a diagram functorially from $F$.

**The standard injectives.** For $\tau\in P$ and a finite-dimensional $k$-vector space $W$ let $I_\tau(W)$ be the diagram with value $W$ at every $\sigma\subseteq\tau$ and $0$ elsewhere, the structure maps being identities where both values are $W$. A diagram map $V\to I_\tau(W)$ is exactly a $k$-linear map $V_\tau\to W$, since its $\tau$-component determines all components and conversely any such linear map extends by the zero maps; therefore $I_\tau(W)$ is injective because $\operatorname{Hom}(-,W)$ is exact. Every diagram $V$ embeds into the finite direct sum $\bigoplus_{\tau\in P}I_\tau(V_\tau)$ by the identity component at $\tau$, a nonzero vector of $V_\tau$ being detected by that component. Hence the finite diagram category has enough injectives and explicit finite injective embeddings, and by [F10] every bounded complex of finite-dimensional diagrams has a bounded injective model whose terms are finite sums of these standard injectives with the stated finite-dimensional ranges.

**Representables.** The diagram $P_\sigma$ has value $k$ on cofaces of $\sigma$ and zero elsewhere, and $\operatorname{Hom}(P_\sigma,V)=V_\sigma$; hence it is projective and these diagrams generate. On $\operatorname{St}(\sigma)$ its realization is canonically constant, since all its diagram maps there are identities. The extension-by-zero adjunction gives $j_{\sigma!}k_{\operatorname{St}(\sigma)}\to q^{-1}P_\sigma$, identity on that star; both sides have zero stalks elsewhere, so this actual morphism is an isomorphism. The finite projective bar construction of [F10] resolves every bounded finite-dimensional diagram complex by a bounded complex of finite sums of these representables.

**Internal derived Hom.** For bounded representatives $A,B$, choose a bounded-below injective replacement $B\to J$. By [F16], $\mathcal Hom^\bullet(A,J)$ represents $R\mathcal Hom(A,B)$ and its derived sections on $U$ represent $R\operatorname{Hom}(A|_U,B|_U)$. The reason ordinary sections suffice in this model is that $\mathcal Hom(A^i,J^j)$ is injective: tensor with a $k$-sheaf is exact stalkwise and its right adjoint is sheaf Hom. There are finitely many $A$-degrees in each Hom degree. Restriction preserves injectives by its exact left adjoint $j_!$. Taking the exact filtered colimit of the section complexes therefore gives $\mathcal H^r(R\mathcal Hom(A,B))_x=\varinjlim_{U\ni x}\operatorname{Hom}_{D(U)}(A|_U,B|_U[r])$. Boundedness will follow from the local finite models.

**Sections on a star.** The generization maps of step 1.3 are locally constant along each face: trivialize the finite-rank restriction near a point of that face, lift its finitely many basis germs to ambient sections, and shrink one neighbourhood where their restrictions to each of the finitely many incident cofaces are constant. Their coface matrices are then constant on that face neighbourhood. Since each face interior is connected, these local matrices define the same transported map throughout it; restrictions through nested faces compose as in step 1.3. For $\sigma\in P$, a section on $\operatorname{St}(\sigma)$ with zero germ at $b_\sigma$ vanishes on a nonempty subset of every incident open simplex, hence on that whole simplex by [F6], so it is zero. **Realized injectives are acyclic on stars.** Put $Z_\tau=|\tau|\cap X$, closed in $X$. The restriction of $q^{-1}I_\tau(W)$ to $Z_\tau$ is canonically constant: the restricted diagram has value $W$ and identity maps everywhere. Its stalks vanish off $Z_\tau$, so the actual closed-inclusion unit of [F8] identifies it with $i_{\tau*}W_{Z_\tau}$. Consequently its cohomology on an open $U$ is the constant-sheaf cohomology of $U\cap Z_\tau$. For $U=\operatorname{St}(\sigma)$ this intersection is empty unless $\sigma\le\tau$; otherwise it is the convex set in $|\tau|$ where all coordinates indexed by $\sigma$ are positive, and cannot meet $D$. It has cohomology $W$ in degree zero and zero above by [F7]. Globally $Z_\tau$ contracts to $b_\tau$: at positive time the segment from a retained point to $b_\tau$ lies in $\tau^\circ$. It has a contractible-open neighbourhood basis, being open in the convex simplex $|\tau|$. Hence its constant-sheaf cohomology is also $W$ in degree zero and zero above. This proves ordinary global and star acyclicity of realized standard injectives and their finite sums. It does not claim that they are injective or c-soft among all sheaves.

**The ordinary equivalence.** The constructions of steps 1.2 and 1.3 are inverse equivalences between finite-dimensional covariant $k$-diagrams on $P$ and sheaves on $X$ whose restriction to every open simplex is locally constant of finite rank. On the diagram side, the reconstruction of $\widehat V$ has $V_\sigma(\widehat V)=(\widehat V)_{b_\sigma}\cong V_\sigma$ by step 1.2, and the generization maps of step 1.3 reproduce the maps of $V$, since the canonical sections over the stars have the prescribed values. On the sheaf side, the canonical morphism $\widehat{V(F)}\to F$ is adjunct to the family $V_\sigma\cong F(\operatorname{St}(\sigma))$ of inverse isomorphisms from step 2.1 and is an isomorphism on stalks by steps 1.2, 1.3 and 2.1, hence an isomorphism by [F2]. Both functors are exact: realization is exact by step 1.2, and reconstruction is exact because a sequence of such sheaves is exact exactly when it is exact at the stalks, which by step 1.3 are the values of the reconstructed diagrams and the generization maps are functorial, so a diagram sequence is exact exactly when the corresponding sheaf sequence is.

**Ordinary cohomology models.** Dualizing the finite projective bar resolution of [F10] on the opposite poset gives a bounded injective model $V\to I$ with terms finite sums of standard injectives. Realization is exact, and step 2.4 makes these terms acyclic for global sections and for every retained star. The acyclic-resolution comparison [F13] consequently gives $R\Gamma(\operatorname{St}(\sigma),q^{-1}V)\simeq I_\sigma\simeq V_\sigma$ and $R\Gamma(X,q^{-1}V)\simeq\lim_{\sigma\in P}I_\sigma$. Here its bounded-complex version follows by resolving the finitely many source degrees and filtering the total complex; the sheaf-level comparisons of [F13] identify each graded piece, hence the total. All syzygies lie in the whole field-sheaf category covered by [F11], and AC supplies DC. This last complex is a bounded finite-dimensional cochain model. Equivalently the bar model of [F10] has incidence terms $\prod_{\sigma_0<\cdots<\sigma_p}V_{\sigma_p}$ and its coefficient and face differential. Its finite matrix construction commutes with every field extension. By step 2.2 this complex is a bounded finite cochain model for the compact-support cohomology $R\Gamma_c(X,q^{-1}V)$, and as in step 3.2 every map in the construction is $k$-linear between finite-dimensional spaces, so the model and hence the cohomology commute with every coefficient field extension by [F10].

**Product comparison and unit.** The acyclic resolution of step 4.1 identifies $R\operatorname{pr}_*\operatorname{pr}^*A$ with $q_V^{-1}I\otimes_kC^\bullet(F;k)$. Naturality and restriction compatibility follow from the diagram maps, the termwise direct-image identification and the canonical acyclic-resolution comparisons; they do not rely on testing all-sheaf stalks on whole stars. The adjunction unit is represented by $B\to I$ tensored with the fibre augmentation $k\to C^\bullet(F;k)$. It is therefore $A\otimes(k\to C^\bullet(F;k))$ under the comparison. After full faithfulness and the essential-image argument below, this applies to every $A$ in the stated constructible subcategory; in the Statement this realized base object is denoted $B$.

**Derived full faithfulness.** For bounded diagram complexes $U,W$, take a finite projective bar model $P\to U$ and an injective replacement $q^{-1}W\to J$. By [F11], [F12] and the inverse/direct-image adjunction, the Hom complex from $q^{-1}P$ to $J$ equals the Hom complex from $P$ to $q_*J$. The derived carrier unit of step 4.2 identifies $q_*J$ with $W$. Since the bounded projective model $P$ is K-projective, taking degree-zero cohomology identifies $\operatorname{Hom}_{D(X)}(q^{-1}U,q^{-1}W)$ with $\operatorname{Hom}_{D(P)}(U,W)$, naturally and compatibly with realization. Shifts give the same comparison in every degree, and [F14] identifies the bounded localizations with their full subcategories. Thus realization is fully faithful.

**The qualified cone estimate.** Suppose in addition that the fibre augmentation $k\to H^0(F;k)$ is an isomorphism (for these finite models, $F$ nonempty and connected), and that $H^r(F;k)=0$ for $1\le r\le R$. Then $\widetilde C=\operatorname{Cone}(k\to C^\bullet(F;k))$ has no cohomology in degrees $\le R$, including degree $-1$. For $A\in D^{\ge b}$, the Künneth formula gives $H^n(A\otimes\widetilde C)=\bigoplus_{p+r=n}H^p(A)\otimes H^r(\widetilde C)$ stalkwise; a nonzero term requires $p\ge b$ and $r\ge R+1$. The cone of the unit therefore lies in $D^{\ge b+R+1}$. Without the degree-zero condition the estimate is false, for example for a two-point fibre and $A=k$: the unit has cokernel $k$ in degree zero. The product comparison itself needs no connectedness condition and remains local to the supplied models.

**Finite Hom and scalar extension.** Full faithfulness identifies actual derived Hom with the finite diagram Hom model of [F10]. Its terms are finite products of $\operatorname{Hom}_k(V_\sigma,W_\tau)$ from finite-dimensional coefficient spaces. Tensor with a field extension commutes with these Hom spaces, finite sums, and the matrices and cohomology of the bounded model. This proves the Hom and scalar-extension clauses. The analytic injective replacement $J$ in step 5.2 need not have finite-dimensional terms; it is the equivalent diagram model that is finite.

**The essential image.** First, if $V$ is a bounded complex of diagrams, then each cohomology sheaf of $q^{-1}V$ is $q^{-1}(H^jV)$ by exactness of $q^{-1}$, and its restriction to an open simplex in $P$ is constant of finite rank, so such complexes lie in the stated image and have bounded finite-rank locally constant cohomology on each open simplex. Conversely, let $A$ be a bounded complex on $X$ whose cohomology sheaves are finite-rank locally constant on every open simplex. By step 3.1 each $H^j(A)$ is isomorphic to $q^{-1}V_j$ for a finite-dimensional diagram $V_j$, and $V_j=0$ outside a finite range of degrees. We build $A$ inductively from its cohomology. If $A$ has at most one nonzero cohomology sheaf, then $A\cong H^n(A)[-n]\cong q^{-1}\bigl(V_n[-n]\bigr)$, using that $q^{-1}$ commutes with shifts up to canonical isomorphism because it is exact. Otherwise let $m$ be the least degree with $H^m(A)\neq0$; the canonical truncation triangle of [F14] reads $H^m(A)[-m]\to A\to\tau^{\ge m+1}A\to H^m(A)[-m+1]$. By induction on the number of nonzero cohomology degrees, $\tau^{\ge m+1}A\cong q^{-1}W$ for a bounded diagram complex $W$, and $H^m(A)[-m]\cong q^{-1}\bigl(V_m[-m]\bigr)$; by step 5.2 the connecting morphism $\delta:q^{-1}W\to q^{-1}(V_m[-m+1])$ is $q^{-1}(\delta_0)$ for a unique morphism $\delta_0$ of the diagram derived category. Completing $\delta_0$ to a distinguished triangle $V_m[-m]\to Y\to W\to V_m[-m+1]$ of [F14] and applying the exact functor $q^{-1}$ yields a triangle $q^{-1}(V_m[-m])\to q^{-1}Y\to q^{-1}W\to q^{-1}(V_m[-m+1])$ whose connecting morphism is $\delta$; two distinguished triangles with isomorphic first two objects and the same connecting morphism are isomorphic, so $A\cong q^{-1}Y$ and $A$ is realized. Hence the essential image is exactly the full subcategory of complexes with bounded finite-rank locally constant cohomology on each open simplex.

**Local internal-Hom models.** For $x\in\sigma^\circ$, sufficiently small ambient Euclidean balls $U$ in $X$ lie in $\operatorname{St}(\sigma)$ and meet exactly the cofaces $Q_\sigma=\{\tau:\tau\ge\sigma\}$. For realized diagram complexes $A=q^{-1}V$, $B=q^{-1}W$, their restrictions are realized by the same restricted diagrams on $Q_\sigma$. The derived carrier-unit argument applies on $U$: for $\eta\le\tau$ in $Q_\sigma$, $U\cap\operatorname{St}(\eta)\cap|\tau|$ is empty or convex, so the restricted standard-injective resolution is acyclic on every restricted principal star. Consequently step 5.2 identifies $\operatorname{Hom}_{D(U)}(A|_U,B|_U[r])$ with the finite diagram Hom cohomology on $Q_\sigma$. Restriction to smaller such balls is the identity on these finite models. No convexity of an entire open star is required. By step 1.6 the stalk of internal Hom is therefore this same finite model. These identifications also prove local constancy along $\sigma^\circ$, rather than only equality of stalk dimensions: a class on one such ball maps canonically into the cohomology sheaf, and its restrictions to smaller balls about nearby points of $\sigma^\circ$ are the identical diagram class. This defines a map from the constant finite-model cohomology sheaf on $U\cap\sigma^\circ$ to the restricted internal-Hom cohomology sheaf, isomorphic on every stalk, hence an isomorphism.

**Boundedness and field extension of internal Hom.** The models $\operatorname{Ext}^q_{\operatorname{Diag}(Q_\sigma)}(V|_{Q_\sigma},W|_{Q_\sigma})$ are finite-dimensional and vanish outside a range depending only on the internal amplitude of $V,W$ and the chain length of $Q_\sigma$, whose strict-chain length is at most that of $P$; since $P$ is finite and $Q_\sigma$ depends only on the simplex $\sigma$, the ranges are uniformly bounded over $\sigma$ and over points of $\sigma^\circ$, so $R\mathcal{H}om(A,B)$ is bounded with finite-rank locally constant cohomology. By [F10] the diagram Hom models commute with every field extension, and the identifications of step 6.4 use only the finite models, so extending scalars carries the internal-Hom models to the models of the extended objects. This proves the internal-Hom clause.

The ordinary equivalence is step 3.1; ordinary cohomology is step 3.2; compact supports are steps 2.2 and 4.3; full faithfulness, finite Hom and the essential image are steps 5.2, 6.2 and 6.3; internal derived Hom is steps 6.4 and 7.1; and the product comparison and qualified cone estimate are steps 5.1 and 6.1. Let $\mathcal F$ be a presheaf on a topological space $X$. We say that
$\mathcal F$ is a **sheaf** if for every open set $U \subseteq X$ and every
open cover $U=\bigcup_{i\in I}U_i$, including the empty cover of
$\varnothing$, the following two conditions hold.

**Locality.** If $s,t\in\mathcal F(U)$ satisfy
$$s|_{U_i}=t|_{U_i}\qquad\text{for all }i\in I,$$
then $s=t$.

**Gluing.** If sections $s_i\in\mathcal F(U_i)$ satisfy
$$s_i|_{U_i\cap U_j}=s_j|_{U_i\cap U_j}\qquad\text{for all }i,j\in I,$$
then there exists $s\in\mathcal F(U)$ such that
$$s|_{U_i}=s_i\qquad\text{for all }i\in I.$$

By locality, such a section $s$ is automatically unique. Thus a sheaf is
exactly a presheaf whose compatible local sections glue uniquely.

Let $X$ be a topological space.
Fix a ring $R$ when modules are under discussion.

A **presheaf of groups** on $X$ is a presheaf $\mathcal F$ such that every
$\mathcal F(U)$ is a group and every restriction map
$\rho^U_V:\mathcal F(U)\to\mathcal F(V)$ is a group homomorphism
([[prop-groups-and-homomorphisms-form-category-grp]]).

A **presheaf of rings** on $X$ is defined the same way with rings and ring
homomorphisms ([[prop-rings-and-homomorphisms-form-category-ring]]).

A **presheaf of left $R$-modules** on $X$ is defined the same way with left
$R$-modules and $R$-linear maps
([[prop-modules-and-homomorphisms-form-category-rmod]]).

A **sheaf of groups**, **sheaf of rings**, or **sheaf of left $R$-modules** is
such a presheaf whose underlying set-valued presheaf is a sheaf.

In particular, each sheaf of groups has a distinguished identity section on
every open set; in additive notation this section is written $0$, and all
restrictions preserve the algebraic operations.

Let $(X,\mathcal O_X)$ be a ringed space.

An **$\mathcal O_X$-module** is a sheaf $\mathcal F$ of abelian groups on $X$
such that for every open set $U \subseteq X$ the section group $\mathcal F(U)$
is an $\mathcal O_X(U)$-module, and for every inclusion $V \subseteq U$ the
restriction map
$$
\mathcal F(U)\longrightarrow\mathcal F(V)
$$
is $\mathcal O_X(U)$-linear after restricting scalars along
$\mathcal O_X(U)\to\mathcal O_X(V)$.

A **morphism of $\mathcal O_X$-modules** is a morphism of the underlying sheaves
of abelian groups whose components are $\mathcal O_X(U)$-linear on every open
set $U$.

Let $X$ be a topological space.

1. The category of sheaves of abelian groups on $X$ is an abelian category.
2. If $(X,\mathcal O_X)$ is a ringed space, then the category of
   $\mathcal O_X$-modules is also an abelian category.

Let
$$
\cdots\longrightarrow \mathcal F_{i-1}\xrightarrow{d_{i-1}}\mathcal F_i\xrightarrow{d_i}\mathcal F_{i+1}\longrightarrow\cdots
$$
be a sequence of sheaves of abelian groups on a topological space $X$. Then the
sequence is exact if and only if, for every point $x\in X$, the stalk sequence
$$
\cdots\longrightarrow (\mathcal F_{i-1})_x\xrightarrow{(d_{i-1})_x}(\mathcal F_i)_x\xrightarrow{(d_i)_x}(\mathcal F_{i+1})_x\longrightarrow\cdots
$$
is exact.

Let $f:X\to Y$ be a continuous map, and let $\mathcal G$ be a presheaf on $Y$.
The **inverse-image presheaf**
$$
f_{\mathrm p}\mathcal G
$$
on $X$ is defined by
$$
(f_{\mathrm p}\mathcal G)(U):=\varinjlim_{f(U)\subseteq V}\mathcal G(V),
$$
where $V$ runs over the open neighbourhoods of $f(U)$ in $Y$, ordered by
reverse inclusion. If $U' \subseteq U$, then every neighbourhood of $f(U)$ is a
neighbourhood of $f(U')$, so there is a natural restriction map
$(f_{\mathrm p}\mathcal G)(U)\to(f_{\mathrm p}\mathcal G)(U')$.

The **inverse image sheaf** of a sheaf $\mathcal G$ on $Y$ is the sheafification
of this presheaf:
$$
f^{-1}\mathcal G:=a(f_{\mathrm p}\mathcal G).
$$

When $U$ is open in $X$ and $V$ is an open set of $Y$ with $f(U)\subseteq V$,
there is a canonical map
$$
\mathcal G(V)\longrightarrow(f_{\mathrm p}\mathcal G)(U)
$$
into the colimit class represented by $V$.

Let $f:X\to Y$ be a continuous map, and let $\mathcal F$ be a presheaf on $X$.
The **direct image presheaf**
$$f_*\mathcal F$$
on $Y$ is defined on an open set $V \subseteq Y$ by
$$
(f_*\mathcal F)(V):=\mathcal F(f^{-1}(V)).
$$
If $V' \subseteq V$, the restriction map
$$
(f_*\mathcal F)(V)\longrightarrow(f_*\mathcal F)(V')
$$
is the restriction map of $\mathcal F$ for the inclusion
$f^{-1}(V') \subseteq f^{-1}(V)$.

Thus direct image is just precomposition of the presheaf with the inverse-image
map on open sets.

Let $f:X\to Y$ be a continuous map.

1. If $\mathcal F$ is a sheaf on $X$, then $f_*\mathcal F$ is a sheaf on $Y$.
2. If $\mathcal F$ is a sheaf of groups, rings, or modules on $X$, then
   $f_*\mathcal F$ is a sheaf of the same kind on $Y$.

Let $f:X\to Y$ be a continuous map, let $\mathcal G$ be a sheaf on $Y$, and let
$\mathcal F$ be a sheaf on $X$. Then there is a natural bijection
$$\operatorname{Hom}_X(f^{-1}\mathcal G,\mathcal F) \cong \operatorname{Hom}_Y(\mathcal G,f_*\mathcal F).$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $X$ be a topological
space and let $k$ be a field. The category $\operatorname{Sh}_k(X)$ of sheaves
of $k$-vector spaces is the category of modules over the ringed space
$(X,k_X)$ with constant structure sheaf $k_X$
([[def-locally-ringed-space]], [[def-module-on-ringed-space]]); it is a locally
small Grothendieck category and carries a functorial injective embedding, and
iterating that embedding on cokernels yields for every $k$-sheaf one specific
injective resolution
([[lem-ringed-space-module-sheaves-enough-injectives]]). Every bounded-below
complex also has a bounded-below termwise injective replacement
([[lem-bounded-below-complexes-admit-injective-replacements]]). With the dependent choice supplied by
AC ([[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]]) the bounded-below
injective complexes model the bounded-below derived category:
$K^+(\operatorname{Inj}\operatorname{Sh}_k(X))\to
D^+(\operatorname{Sh}_k(X))$ is an equivalence
([[thm-injective-complexes-model-the-bounded-below-derived-category]]).
Its full subcategory of bounded-below injective complexes with bounded
cohomology models $D^b(\operatorname{Sh}_k(X))$, and morphisms of the bounded
derived category are computed by these replacements; the replacements need
not have bounded terms.

Now let $X$ be a separated finite-type complex algebraic variety and let
$\mathfrak S$ be a finite smooth algebraic stratification with the frontier
condition of $X$
([[def-analytic-topology-and-finite-smooth-algebraic-stratifications]]). Let
$D^b_{\mathfrak S}(X;k)$ be the full subcategory of
$D^b(\operatorname{Sh}_k(X))$ of complexes whose cohomology sheaves are bounded
and constructible with respect to $\mathfrak S$
([[def-algebraically-constructible-complex-of-analytic-field-sheaves]]). Then
$D^b_{\mathfrak S}(X;k)$ is a triangulated subcategory: it is closed under
shifts, isomorphisms and mapping cones. More generally, if two bounded
algebraically constructible complexes are constructible with respect to one
common finite smooth algebraic frontier stratification, then their cone is
bounded and constructible with respect to that stratification.

With supplied bounded-below injective replacements $j_X:X\to I_X$ (and DC or supplied homotopy extensions), $K^+(\operatorname{Inj}\mathcal A)\to D^+(\mathcal A)$ is an equivalence of triangulated categories. For a bounded-below complex $I$, K-injectivity can be tested using only bounded-below acyclic inputs.
A bounded-below cochain complex $I$ of injective objects is K-injective. Assume dependent choice for the countable successive homotopy extensions, or supply those extensions as data.

A cochain complex $I$ is **homotopically injective**, or **K-injective**, if $\operatorname{Hom}_K(A,I[r])=0$ for every acyclic cochain complex $A$ and every integer $r$. Equivalently, $\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}(A,I)$ is acyclic. This uses the Hom complex and shifted Hom identification fixed in [[def-homotopically-projective-bounded-above-complex]]. A **bounded-below K-injective complex** additionally has $I^n=0$ for all sufficiently negative $n$. The K-injective property itself neither assumes boundedness nor means termwise injectivity.

For a K-injective complex $I$ and any complex $X$, $Q:\operatorname{Hom}_K(X,I)\to\operatorname{Hom}_D(X,I)$ is bijective. Moreover, if $s:I\to J$ is a quasi-isomorphism, its cone triangle is split in $K$: $J\cong I\oplus\operatorname{Cone}(s)$ with $s$ corresponding to the inclusion.

If $\mathcal A$ has enough injectives and $X^n=0$ for $n<a$, there is a termwise monic quasi-isomorphism $j:X\to I$ with each $I^n$ injective and $I^n=0$ for $n<a$. Let $\mathcal A$ be an abelian category. A **cochain complex in $\mathcal A$**
is a family of objects $(C^n)_{n\in\mathbb Z}$ together with morphisms
$$d^n:C^n\to C^{n+1}$$
such that
$$d^{n+1}\circ d^n=0$$
for every $n\in\mathbb Z$.

This page uses the reindexing convention that a cochain complex $C^\bullet$ may
also be read as the chain complex with $(C^\sharp)_n:=C^{-n}$ and
$d^\sharp_n:=d^{-n}$, so that lower and upper indices differ only by the sign
of the grading.

Let $C$ be a [[def-homological-double-complex|homological double complex]] in
an abelian category. Suppose that for every integer $n$ the diagonal
[[def-products-and-coproducts|coproduct]] below exists, and write its injections
as $\iota^n_{p,q}$:
$$T_n=\operatorname{Tot}^{\oplus}_n(C)=\coprod_{p+q=n}C_{p,q}.$$
Define $d_n:T_n\to T_{n-1}$ to be the unique arrow with
$$d_n\iota^n_{p,q}=\iota^{n-1}_{p-1,q}h_{p,q}+\iota^{n-1}_{p,q-1}v_{p,q}\quad(p+q=n).$$
Each right-hand side is the sum of two morphisms with the same source and
target. The coproduct universal property supplies a unique $d_n$ from this
family; no infinite sum in a morphism group is required.

The resulting **direct-sum total complex** has differential of degree $-1$.
Its chain condition is established in
[[lem-the-total-differential-squares-to-zero]]. A diagonal with only zero
objects has zero coproduct: every family of maps from its objects is the
unique zero family. A diagonal with exactly one nonzero object has that
object as coproduct. For general infinite diagonals existence is a hypothesis,
not an implication of being an abelian category. No choices of elements or
representatives enter this construction.

For the direct-sum totalisation of an anticommuting homological double
complex, $d_{n-1}d_n=0$ for every integer $n$.

Let K be a cochain complex with decreasing filtration by subcomplexes. Set $C_n=K^{-n}$, $F_pC_n=F^{-p}K^{-n}$ and $d_n=d_K^{-n}$. Then

The construction gives $E_0^{p,q}=\operatorname{gr}^p K^{p+q}$ and $E_1^{p,q}\cong H^{p+q}(\operatorname{gr}^p K)$. With degreewise finite filtration it naturally abuts to the decreasing image filtration on $H^{p+q}(K)$, with $E_\infty^{p,q}\cong\operatorname{gr}^pH^{p+q}(K)$.

For a cochain complex $X$, define the **canonical truncations** by

$$ (\tau^{\leq n}X)^i=\begin{cases}X^i&i<n,\\\ker d_X^n&i=n,\\0&i>n,\end{cases}\qquad (\tau^{\geq n}X)^i=\begin{cases}0&i<n,\\\operatorname{coker}d_X^{n-1}&i=n,\\X^i&i>n.\end{cases} $$

The differential into $\ker d_X^n$ is the factorization of $d_X^{n-1}$; the differential out of $\operatorname{coker}d_X^{n-1}$ is induced by $d_X^n$. All other retained differentials are those of $X$. There are natural maps $\tau^{\leq n}X\to X\to\tau^{\geq n}X$. Unlike [[def-brutal-truncation-of-a-complex]], these constructions correct the boundary using the cycle and boundary objects of [[def-cohomology-object-of-a-cochain-complex]].

Every short exact sequence $0\to A\xrightarrow iB\xrightarrow qC\to0$ of cochain complexes gives a natural distinguished triangle $A\to B\to C\to A[1]$ in $D(\mathcal A)$. In particular, for every integer $n$ there are canonical distinguished triangles

$$\tau^{\leq n}X\to X\to\tau^{\geq n+1}X\to(\tau^{\leq n}X)[1],$$

$$\tau^{\leq n}X\to\tau^{\leq n+1}X\to H^{n+1}(X)[-n-1]\to(\tau^{\leq n}X)[1],$$

$$H^n(X)[-n]\to\tau^{\geq n}X\to\tau^{\geq n+1}X\to H^n(X)[-n+1].$$

The derived category, with shift $[1]$ and distinguished triangles the isomorphic images of cone triangles, is triangulated. The localization functor $Q$ is exact. Every such triangle gives a long exact cohomology sequence $\cdots\to H^n(X)\to H^n(Y)\to H^n(Z)\to H^{n+1}(X)\to\cdots$.

The canonical functors $D^-(\mathcal A),D^+(\mathcal A),D^b(\mathcal A)\to D(\mathcal A)$ are fully faithful and exact. Their essential images consist exactly of complexes with cohomology respectively bounded above, bounded below, or bounded on both sides.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Constructibility is a condition on the cohomology sheaves of a complex, and it

stratifications: no stratification is fixed, and no existence or

Shifting replaces $H^j$ by $H^{j+m}$, which preserves cohomological boundedness

presheaf** with value $A$, $A_{\mathrm{pt}}(U)=A$ for every open $U$ with all
restriction maps the identity ([[def-presheaf-on-topological-space]]), and let
$$A_X:=aA_{\mathrm{pt}}$$

value $A$ on $X$. Then:

   constant}\}$, with the usual restriction maps, is a sheaf of sets on $X$, and
   for every $x\in X$ evaluation at $x$ is a canonical bijection
   $\underline A_{\mathrm{loc},x}\cong A$
   ([[lem-locally-constant-functions-form-a-sheaf]]);

   $\eta:A_{\mathrm{pt}}\to A_X$ is the sheafification map;

   $a\mapsto\text{the constant function with value }a$ are group homomorphisms,
